The paper presents a 'complete' ULLT model based on the framework of Sclavounos, and two simplified ULLT models with different wake assumptions.
The CFD simulations were performed for NACA 0004 rectangular wings with aspect ratios of 2, 4, and 8, and chord-based reduced frequencies (k) ranging from 0.1 to 1.0.
The 'complete' ULLT model showed good agreement with the Euler CFD results for whole wing lift and pitching moment coefficients across the range of aspect ratios and frequencies tested.
The simplified ULLT models, which used either a pseudosteady or simplified wake model, were less accurate than the 'complete' ULLT, particularly at higher frequencies.
Accounting for the harmonic variation of streamwise wake vorticity was found to be important for accurately predicting the spanwise distribution of loads, especially at higher frequencies.

The paper establishes ULLT as a low-cost model capable of capturing the interacting finite-wing and oscillation frequency effects, and identifies the regimes where the different ULLT models are most accurate.
The research paves the way towards the construction of time-domain or numerical ULLTs that may be augmented to account for non-linearities such as flow separation.
Previous validations of ULLT have been limited to comparisons with unsteady vortex lattice methods, which share some assumptions with ULLT.
This work is the first to validate ULLT against high-fidelity Euler CFD simulations, which avoid the explicit assumptions of vortex lattice methods.
The paper suggests that the pseudosteady wake assumption, commonly used in time-domain lifting-line models, is only asymptotically valid in the very low frequency regime.
The 'complete' ULLT model was found to be most accurate for span-scale wake wavelengths and longer, corresponding to the very low and low frequency regimes.
The simplified ULLT models became less accurate as the frequency increased and the assumption of a uniform downwash broke down.
The paper also compares the ULLT models to experimental data, confirming their relevance even when the flow is not inviscid before separation.
The research provides insights into the trade-off between wake model complexity and ULLT accuracy, which is useful for developing more advanced numerical ULLTs.
The paper lays the groundwork for future work on time-domain or numerical ULLTs that can account for non-linearities and flow separation.
